plain: Several passages in the Hebrew Bible picture God presiding over a heavenly assembly of lesser spiritual beings, called "sons of God", "holy ones" or even "gods" (elohim). Psalm 82 is the clearest example: God stands up in "the divine council" and judges the gods who have ruled the nations unjustly. Many scholars, including the late Michael Heiser, think this "divine council" idea is a key to reading the whole Bible story, from Babel and the scattering of the nations to Pentecost and the nations healed in Revelation. Others agree the council imagery is real but read some of the key texts differently: "let us" in Genesis 1:26 as a hint of the Trinity or a plural of majesty, the "gods" of Psalm 82 as human judges, and the "sons of God" of Genesis 6 as godly men from Seth's line. Critical historians such as Mark Smith see the council as a leftover from an older Israelite religion that only slowly became monotheistic. All of these readings agree on one thing the texts state plainly: in the Bible, Yahweh alone is Creator, has no equal, and is the only one to be worshipped.
keyPoints: "Elohim" (usually translated "God" or "gods") is used in the Hebrew Bible for the God of Israel, for foreign gods, for members of God's heavenly assembly and once even for the ghost of Samuel, so the word alone does not tell you which being is meant.

Psalm 82, 1 Kings 22, Job 1–2, Isaiah 6, Psalm 89 and Daniel 7 all describe God surrounded by a heavenly court; this much is widely agreed, since the imagery has close parallels in the Ugaritic texts about El's assembly (found from 1929).

Deuteronomy 32:8 is a famous text-critical puzzle: the traditional Hebrew text says the nations were divided by the number of "the sons of Israel", but a Dead Sea Scroll and the Greek Septuagint point to "the sons of God"; many modern versions now follow the older reading.

On the divine-council reading, the Bible tells a story of three rebellions (Eden, Genesis 6 and Babel), after which the nations were handed over to lesser gods while Yahweh took Israel as his own portion.

That reading sees the New Testament as the reclaiming of the nations: Jesus disarms the "rulers and authorities" (Col 2:15), Pentecost reverses Babel (Acts 2) and Revelation ends with every nation worshipping the Lamb.

Critics accept parts of the picture but question others: whether "let us" means a council, whether Psalm 82's "gods" are angels or human judges, whether Genesis 6 speaks of angels, and whether Isaiah's "there is no other" denies that any other gods exist.

The council members are always presented as created and subordinate: they are commanded to worship Yahweh, can be judged by him, and in Psalm 82 are told they will "die like men". Nobody in the debate thinks the Bible teaches worship of more than one God.

The word "monotheism" is a modern label (17th century), so scholars argue about whether it fits ancient Israel; the real question is how to describe a faith that insists on one Creator while speaking of other heavenly beings.

tiers.name: Yahweh, the Most High
tiers.who: The God of Israel, the Creator, called Elyon ("Most High"), "God of gods and Lord of lords" and "great King above all gods". He presides over the assembly and is never one member among equals.
tiers.role: Creates, rules, judges the other heavenly beings, and receives worship. Council readers stress that he is unique in kind, not just top of a ladder; the Bible says he alone made the heavens and their host. In the New Testament the early Christians (on the reading of Richard Bauckham and Larry Hurtado) included Jesus within this unique divine identity, not among the lesser beings.

tiers.name: Sons of God (bene elohim)
tiers.hebrew: בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים / בְּנֵי אֵלִים (bene ha-elohim, bene elim)
tiers.who: Heavenly beings called "sons of God", "holy ones", "the host of heaven" and sometimes "gods". They are present at creation, appear before Yahweh in Job's court and, on many readings, are the "gods" judged in Psalm 82.
tiers.role: Members of the heavenly court who deliberate and carry out tasks. On the council reading (Heiser and others), some were given oversight of the nations (Deut 32:8 in its older form), ruled unjustly, and lie behind the "princes" of Persia and Greece in Daniel and Paul's "rulers and authorities". Others read most of these texts as describing angels in general without a distinct ruling tier, or (for Psalm 82) as human judges. Ellen White and others question whether the Bible has fixed "tiers" at all.

tiers.name: Messengers (angels)
tiers.who: "Messengers": the Hebrew mal'ak, like the Greek angelos, describes a job rather than a kind of being, and is also used of human messengers. Examples are the visitors to Abraham, the angels on Jacob's ladder, Gabriel and Michael.
tiers.role: Carry messages and do God's errands among humans: announcing, protecting, guiding and sometimes judging. Heiser treats "messenger" as a lower working rank under the sons of God; many other scholars think the Bible uses "sons of God", "holy ones" and "angels" for one broad group seen from different sides (the Greek Old Testament often translates "sons of God" as "angels").

tiers.name: Throne attendants: cherubim, seraphim, living creatures
tiers.who: Composite guardian beings around God's throne: cherubim guarding Eden and shaped on the ark's lid, seraphim ("burning ones") in Isaiah's vision, and the four "living creatures" of Ezekiel and Revelation. Similar winged guardians flanked thrones and temples across the ancient Near East.
tiers.role: Guard God's holy presence, carry his throne-chariot, and lead worship ("Holy, holy, holy"). They are not shown governing nations or deliberating; they mark the space around the throne. Ezekiel identifies his living creatures as cherubim.

elohimUses.note: "In the beginning God (elohim) created..." By far the commonest use: well over 2,000 of the roughly 2,600 occurrences refer to Israel's God. The form is plural but takes a singular verb here, which is why most grammarians call it a plural of majesty or "fullness" when used of Israel's God.

The medium at En-dor says, "I see elohim coming up out of the earth." The ghost of a dead human is called elohim, which shows the word can mean a being from the spirit world rather than "deity" in the full sense. Heiser called it a "place of residence" term; others call it simply a broad word for supernatural beings.

Jephthah tells the Ammonite king, "Will you not possess what Chemosh your god (elohim) gives you?" He argues on the other side's terms; scholars differ on whether this reflects Jephthah's real belief, diplomatic rhetoric, or simply ordinary speech about foreign gods.

"God (elohim) stands in the divine council; in the midst of the gods (elohim) he holds judgment." The same word appears twice in one verse with two different referents: first the God of Israel (singular verb), then the beings he judges.

elohimUses.who: The "gods" addressed as sons of the Most High
elohimUses.note: "I said, 'You are gods (elohim), sons of the Most High, all of you.'" Read as heavenly beings by most modern scholars and as human judges (or Israel at Sinai) in much older Jewish and Christian interpretation. Jesus quotes this verse in John 10:34.

"On all the gods (elohe) of Egypt I will execute judgments." The plagues are framed as judgment on Egypt's gods (also Num 33:4). Whether the writer means real spiritual powers, the idols and cult, or both is itself part of the debate.

A slave who wants to stay is brought "to ha-elohim". The KJV and some others render "the judges"; the ESV, NRSV and most recent versions render "to God", meaning before God at the sanctuary. The "judges" reading is one support for the human-judges view of Psalm 82; many scholars think it is not needed here (compare Exod 22:8-9).

Humans are made "a little lower than elohim". The Greek Septuagint and the KJV have "angels" (followed by Heb 2:7); the NRSV and NASB have "God"; the ESV has "the heavenly beings". Both are grammatically possible.

elohimUses.who: The gods who must bow to Yahweh
elohimUses.note: Yahweh is "God of gods (elohe ha-elohim) and Lord of lords". Compare Ps 97:7, "worship him, all you gods" (the Greek has "all his angels", quoted in Heb 1:6 by way of Deut 32:43). Council readers take these as real beings; others take them as a superlative way of saying "the supreme God".
Ashtoreth (Astarte) is called the elohim of the Sidonians. Biblical Hebrew has no separate common word for "goddess", so elohim covers female deities too.

scenes.title: "Let us make humankind"
scenes.setting: The sixth day of creation, just before humans are made. Up to now God has spoken in the singular ("Let there be light").
scenes.whatHappens: God says, "Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness," and then the narrative says God (singular) created humankind in his image. The switch to "us" and back has puzzled readers since antiquity. Job 38:7 adds that "the sons of God" shouted for joy at the founding of the earth, so heavenly beings are imagined as present at creation.

readings.text: God announces his decision to the heavenly court, as kings do to their courtiers (compare 1 Kgs 22:20; Isa 6:8). He alone creates (v. 27 uses a singular verb), but humans share an "image" with the heavenly family. Held by many modern commentators, critical and conservative (Heiser among them), and anticipated by ancient Jewish interpreters such as Philo and later rabbinic readings in which God consults the angels.

The plural hints at plurality within the one God: Father, Word and Spirit (the Spirit is present in Gen 1:2; John 1:3 and Col 1:16 put the Son at creation). This was the dominant reading of the Church Fathers (e.g. Irenaeus, Augustine) and the Reformers. Critics note that Hebrew readers would not have taken it this way; defenders reply that later revelation can show the fuller meaning of an earlier text.

God speaks to himself, either as a royal "we" or as someone deliberating ("let's see"). Supporters point to the singular verbs around it; critics note that a royal "we" with verbs is not clearly attested in biblical Hebrew and that the "us" in Gen 3:22 ("like one of us") is hard to explain as self-talk.

scenes.title: "Like one of us" and "Let us go down"
scenes.setting: Two more plural speeches: after the fall in Eden (Gen 3:22) and at the tower of Babel (Gen 11:7).
scenes.whatHappens: After Adam and Eve eat, Yahweh says, "The man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil" and bars the way to the tree of life, which cherubim then guard (Gen 3:22-24). At Babel he says, "Come, let us go down and confuse their language" (Gen 11:7), scattering the peoples who then appear as the nations of Genesis 10.

readings.text: "One of us" means one of the heavenly beings who already know good and evil; at Babel the council acts with Yahweh, which sets up the allotting of the nations in Deut 32:8-9. Heiser treats Babel as the third great rebellion.
Classical Christian readers took both as further hints of the Trinity, since in Gen 11:5 it is Yahweh who comes down.
God talks to himself, as in Gen 1:26; Gen 11:7 echoes the builders' own "Come, let us" (Gen 11:3-4) as a deliberate ironic parallel, which may explain the plural without a council.

scenes.title: The sons of God present themselves (Job)
scenes.setting: A day when "the sons of God" come to present themselves before Yahweh, like officials reporting at court (repeated in Job 2:1-7).
scenes.whatHappens: Among the sons of God comes ha-satan, who has been roaming the earth. Yahweh points to Job's integrity; the accuser asks whether Job fears God "for nothing" and is allowed to test him within limits Yahweh sets. Job 38:7 adds that the sons of God shouted for joy at creation.

readings.text: A court scene: the members report and one plays a prosecutor's role. The Hebrew has the article ("the satan"), so it is probably a title, not yet a personal name; compare Zech 3:1-2. On this view the figure later identified as Satan develops from this role.
The adversary is Satan himself, already fallen but still permitted access to God's court under strict control (compare Rev 12:10, "the accuser of our brothers").

Many scholars treat the heavenly prologue as a literary frame that sets up the book's question (does anyone serve God for nothing?) rather than as a report of heavenly events. This is compatible with either of the above.

scenes.title: Micaiah sees the host of heaven
scenes.setting: Kings Ahab of Israel and Jehoshaphat of Judah plan war at Ramoth-gilead; 400 prophets promise victory. The prophet Micaiah describes a vision.
whoIsThere: All the host of heaven on his right and left
scenes.whatHappens: Yahweh asks, "Who will entice Ahab?" Members of the host offer different proposals until a spirit volunteers to be "a lying spirit" in the prophets' mouths, and Yahweh sends it. Ahab ignores the warning and dies in battle (1 Kgs 22:34-37).

readings.text: The clearest picture of the council deliberating: Yahweh decides the outcome, but invites proposals and delegates the means. Many critical and conservative scholars alike accept this description of the scene.

Commentators wrestle with God sending a deceiving spirit. Common answers: it is judgment on a king who already rejected the truth (compare 2 Thess 2:11); Micaiah openly tells Ahab the plan, so Ahab is warned; or the vision is a dramatic way of saying God has handed Ahab over to his chosen prophets.
Some, ancient and modern, read the vision as a parable Micaiah is shown rather than a literal heavenly meeting.

scenes.title: Isaiah in the throne room
scenes.setting: "In the year King Uzziah died" (about 740 BC), Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned, the hem of his robe filling the temple.
whoIsThere: The Lord (Adonai) on a high throne
scenes.whatHappens: Isaiah cries that he is lost, a man of unclean lips; a seraph touches his lips with a coal from the altar. The Lord asks, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Isaiah answers, "Here am I; send me" and receives his commission.

readings.text: Like Micaiah's vision, a prophet stands in the council and hears its decision; "for us" refers to the court. Jeremiah later says false prophets have not "stood in the council (sod) of Yahweh" (Jer 23:18, 22), which suggests that a true prophet's call meant access to this court.
John 12:41 says Isaiah "saw his glory" (Christ's), and Acts 28:25 attributes the words to the Holy Spirit; many Fathers and Reformers took "us" as Trinitarian.
The plural is a royal or deliberative form, as some explain Gen 1:26.

scenes.title: The mount of assembly
scenes.setting: A taunt song against the king of Babylon (Isa 14:4), full of mythic language.
whoIsThere: The "Day Star, son of Dawn" (Helel ben Shachar)
scenes.whatHappens: The arrogant figure says, "I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north (Zaphon)... I will make myself like the Most High" (Isa 14:13-14). Instead he is brought down to Sheol.

readings.view: Mythic background used for a human king
readings.text: Most commentators see a Canaanite-style myth (a lesser star-god trying to climb to the top of the divine mountain; Zaphon was Baal's mountain in the Ugaritic texts) used to mock the Babylonian king. The "mount of assembly" is the place where the council meets.

From Origen and Tertullian on, many Christians read the passage as also describing Satan's fall (the Latin "Lucifer" comes from the Vulgate's rendering of "Day Star"), often linking it with Luke 10:18. Critics reply that the text names the king of Babylon; defenders argue the language goes beyond any human king.
Heiser and others take the human king to be described in terms of a rebellious divine being, so the passage is about both levels at once, as in Ezek 28.

scenes.title: God judges the gods
scenes.setting: A psalm of Asaph set in "the divine council" (Hebrew adat-el, "the assembly of El"), a phrase with close Ugaritic parallels.
scenes.whatHappens: God accuses the gods of judging unjustly and favouring the wicked instead of defending the weak, the fatherless and the poor. Because of this, "the foundations of the earth are shaken." He declares, "You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die." The psalmist ends: "Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations."

readings.text: The gods are heavenly beings set over the nations (connecting to Deut 32:8-9) who have failed; God sentences them to mortality and the psalm prays that he will take the nations back. This is the majority view of modern critical scholars (e.g. Hans-Joachim Kraus, Marvin Tate) and central to Heiser's reading.

The "gods" are Israel's judges, called elohim because they judge on God's behalf (compare Exod 22:28; 2 Chr 19:6). This was common in older rabbinic and Christian interpretation (e.g. Calvin) and is still held by some evangelical scholars, who note the moral charges are about human courts and that "die like men" can mean "die like ordinary people".

Some rabbinic texts read the psalm as addressed to Israel, who became "gods" (immortal) on receiving the law but lost that status through the golden calf. Some scholars think this reading lies behind John 10:34-36.

scenes.title: The assembly of the holy ones
scenes.setting: A royal psalm praising God's faithfulness to David's line.
scenes.whatHappens: The heavens praise Yahweh's wonders "in the assembly of the holy ones". "Who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh? Who among the sons of God is like Yahweh, a God greatly feared in the council of the holy ones?"

readings.text: Almost all interpreters accept that the holy ones are heavenly beings; the point is that none of them compares to Yahweh. Council readers stress that such a comparison only makes sense if the others are real.
Some read the heavenly assembly here as poetic praise language (the heavens themselves praising) rather than evidence for a structured council.

scenes.title: The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man
scenes.setting: Daniel's vision of four beasts rising from the sea, representing successive empires.
whoIsThere: One like a son of man
scenes.whatHappens: Thrones are set in place (plural), the Ancient of Days sits, "the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened." The beasts are judged. Then one "like a son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting dominion over all peoples, nations and languages. Daniel elsewhere calls heavenly beings "watchers" and "holy ones" who issue decrees (Dan 4:17).

readings.text: Jesus applies the scene to himself at his trial (Mark 14:62), and the early church read the son of man as Christ, who receives the nations' dominion. This is the classical Christian reading.

The interpretation in the chapter links the kingdom to "the people of the saints of the Most High" (Dan 7:27), so many scholars think the figure represents faithful Israel, or Israel's angelic patron Michael (John J. Collins argues for an angelic figure).

The plural thrones show a court; the riding on clouds is language elsewhere used of Yahweh (Ps 104:3), so the son of man is a second divine figure. Heiser and others argue this "two powers" pattern prepares for the New Testament's divine Christ.

scenes.title: The morning stars sing at creation
scenes.setting: God's speech from the whirlwind, answering Job.
scenes.whatHappens: God asks Job where he was when the earth's foundations were laid, "when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy." The heavenly beings are witnesses to creation, not helpers in it.

readings.text: The sons of God existed before the earth and were present when it was made, which council readers link to the "us" of Gen 1:26.

Stars and sons of God are parallel, so some read it as poetic praise by the heavens (as in Ps 148:2-3), not a description of a council. Ancient readers widely linked stars and angels (compare Rev 1:20).

scenes.title: The throne room and the Lamb
scenes.setting: John is called up through an open door in heaven and sees the throne of God.
whoIsThere: The One seated on the throne
scenes.whatHappens: The elders and living creatures worship the Creator. No one can open the sealed scroll until the Lamb, the Lion of Judah, takes it. They sing that by his blood he ransomed people "from every tribe and language and people and nation" and made them a kingdom and priests who will reign on the earth. All creation worships God and the Lamb together.

readings.text: The council scene of Dan 7 is replayed: the thrones are now filled partly by redeemed humans (the elders), and the nations once scattered at Babel are gathered by the Lamb. Believers share Christ's throne (Rev 3:21).

Most commentators (e.g. Richard Bauckham) stress that the scene places the Lamb on the divine side of the line between God and creatures, since he receives worship that angels refuse (Rev 19:10; Rev 22:8-9). The elders are variously read as angels, representatives of the twelve tribes and twelve apostles, or the whole people of God.

deut32.mt: The Masoretic Text (the standard medieval Hebrew text, as in the Leningrad Codex of about AD 1008) reads: "When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance, when he divided mankind, he fixed the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel (bene yisra'el)."
deut32.dss: A Hebrew manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, 4QDeut-j (4Q37, first century BC), preserves the end of the verse as "sons of God" (bny 'lwhym, bene elohim). Another small Qumran fragment (4QDeut-q) does not cover verse 8, but it does show a longer form of Deut 32:43 that also mentions heavenly beings, which supports the idea that the poem originally spoke of the heavenly host.
deut32.lxx: The Greek Septuagint (third–second century BC) reads "according to the number of the angels of God" (angelon theou) in most manuscripts; a few manuscripts have "sons of God" (huion theou), which the critical Göttingen edition (J. W. Wevers) prints as the original Greek. Either way, the Greek translators were reading a Hebrew text that referred to heavenly beings, not to Israel.

translations.name: KJV (1611)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the children of Israel" (follows the Masoretic Text)

translations.name: NKJV (1982)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the children of Israel" (Masoretic Text)

translations.name: NASB
translations.reads: "according to the number of the sons of Israel" (Masoretic Text)

translations.name: NIV (2011)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the sons of Israel", with a footnote giving the Dead Sea Scrolls/Septuagint reading "sons of God"

translations.name: RSV (1952)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the sons of God" (the first major English version to adopt the older reading)

translations.name: ESV (2001)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the sons of God", with a footnote noting the Masoretic "sons of Israel"

translations.name: NRSV (1989)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the gods" (following the Qumran/Greek sense)

translations.name: NET (2005)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the heavenly assembly" (following the Qumran/Greek sense, with a long note)

translations.name: CSB (2017)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the people of Israel" (Masoretic Text), with a footnote on the alternative

translations.name: LXX (Greek)
translations.reads: "according to the number of the angels of God" (some manuscripts: "sons of God")

deut32.explanation: Most textual critics, including many conservative ones, now think "sons of God" is the older reading and "sons of Israel" a later change. Three reasons are usually given. First, the oldest witnesses (the Qumran scroll and the Greek) agree against the medieval text. Second, "sons of Israel" fits awkwardly: Israel did not yet exist when the nations were divided (Gen 10–11), and verse 9 sets Israel apart as Yahweh's own portion, distinct from the other nations. Third, a scribe is more likely to have changed "sons of God" to "sons of Israel" (to avoid a reading that seemed to give other gods authority over the nations) than the other way round. Defenders of the Masoretic reading reply that Jewish tradition linked the seventy nations of Gen 10 to the seventy people of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:27; Exod 1:5; Deut 10:22), so "sons of Israel" makes sense in its own way; and that some versions and commentators keep the received text out of respect for it, while noting the alternative.
deut32.significance: With "sons of God", the verse says that when the nations were divided (most connect this with Babel, Gen 11), God set their boundaries according to the number of heavenly beings, while keeping Israel for himself (Deut 32:9). Read with Deut 4:19-20 and Deut 29:26, where the nations' worship of the "host of heaven" seems to be allotted or permitted, and Dan 10:13, 20-21, where "princes" of Persia and Greece oppose Michael, this becomes the backbone of the divine-council reading: the nations were handed over to lesser powers, who then became corrupt (Ps 82), and the gospel reclaims them. Scholars who accept the text-critical point do not all accept that whole theology: some read the verse simply as saying God's ordering of the world matches the structure of his heavenly court, without saying those beings rule the nations; others note that Deut 4:19 can mean God allowed, rather than appointed, the nations' star-worship.

rebellions.title: The serpent in Eden
rebellions.who: The serpent (Hebrew nachash), "more crafty than any other beast of the field". Genesis itself does not call it Satan; the identification is made explicitly in Rev 12:9 and 20:2 ("that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan") and is assumed in Second Temple texts such as Wisdom of Solomon 2:24.
rebellions.what: The serpent questions God's word and tells the woman she will "be like God (or gods), knowing good and evil". The humans eat, are expelled from the garden, and lose access to the tree of life; cherubim guard the way back. Heiser suggests nachash carries a triple wordplay: "serpent", "diviner" (from the verb nachash, to practise divination, Gen 44:5) and "shining one" (linked to nechoshet, bronze; compare Num 21:9). Most lexicons and commentators accept only "serpent" as the meaning here and regard the wordplay as possible but unproven. Some (Heiser among them) link the scene with Ezek 28:13-17, where a figure "in Eden, the garden of God", an "anointed guardian cherub", is cast down for pride; the passage is addressed to the king of Tyre, and the Hebrew and Greek even differ over whether the king is the cherub or was with the cherub.
rebellions.consequence: Death and exile from God's presence for humankind; a curse on the serpent, who is cast down to "eat dust" (a common image for humiliation and the underworld); and lasting hostility between the serpent's offspring and the woman's.
rebellions.reversal: Gen 3:15 promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head while being struck on the heel; Christians from Irenaeus on call it the "first gospel" (protoevangelium). Paul promises that God "will soon crush Satan under your feet" (Rom 16:20); the cross disarms the powers (Col 2:15); Revelation shows the dragon thrown down and finally thrown into the lake of fire (Rev 12:9; 20:10), and the tree of life is open again (Rev 22:2).

readings.text: The serpent is Satan or his instrument; this has been the standard Christian and much Jewish reading since the Second Temple period, building on Rev 12:9 and John 8:44 ("a murderer from the beginning").

The nachash is a member of God's heavenly household, a throne guardian who resented humans being made God's image-bearers and turned them against God. Ezek 28 and Isa 14 are read as echoing this primal fall.

Many critical scholars read the serpent as simply a clever animal in a story about human disobedience, the origin of mortality and why snakes crawl; the link to Satan is a later development. Jewish interpretation varies, often stressing the human evil inclination over a cosmic adversary.

rebellions.title: The sons of God and the Nephilim
rebellions.who: "The sons of God" (bene ha-elohim) who "saw that the daughters of man were attractive" and took wives; the Nephilim ("fallen ones" or possibly "giants") who were on the earth "in those days, and also afterward", the "mighty men of old, men of renown".
rebellions.what: In four compressed verses, the sons of God take human wives; God limits human life to 120 years; the Nephilim are mentioned; and the flood story begins with the world's wickedness (Gen 6:5). The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 6–16, probably third century BC) expands this: 200 angelic "Watchers" led by Shemihazah swear an oath on Mount Hermon, marry women, teach forbidden arts (weapons, sorcery, astrology), and father giants who devour the earth. Jude 1:6 and 2 Pet 2:4 (which uses the Greek verb for consigning to Tartarus) refer to angels who sinned, left their proper dwelling and are kept in chains until judgment, and Jude 1:14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, so most scholars think these letters know the Enochic story. Nephilim reappear in the spies' report about Canaan (Num 13:33), linked with the Anakim and Rephaim (Deut 2:10-11; Deut 3:11).
rebellions.consequence: The spread of violence and corruption that leads to the flood (Gen 6:5-13); in the Enochic tradition, the imprisonment of the Watchers and the release of evil spirits from the giants' bodies (1 Enoch 15:8-12). In the biblical text, the later giant clans of Canaan who must be faced in the conquest.
rebellions.reversal: On the council reading, the imprisoned spirits are those to whom Christ "proclaimed" his victory (1 Pet 3:19-20, read with 1 Enoch), and the angels who sinned are kept for judgment, which believers will share (1 Cor 6:3). Others read 1 Pet 3:19 as Christ preaching through Noah to people of Noah's day, or as a descent to the dead; the passage is one of the most debated in the New Testament.

readings.text: The sons of God are heavenly beings, as the phrase means in Job 1:6, 2:1 and 38:7. This is the oldest attested reading: 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Dead Sea Scrolls, Josephus (*Antiquities* 1.73) and Philo (who allegorises it), and early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr (*2 Apology* 5), Athenagoras, Irenaeus and Tertullian. Most modern critical scholars (e.g. Ronald Hendel) and many evangelicals hold it. Objection: Jesus says angels "neither marry nor are given in marriage" (Matt 22:30); reply: he speaks of angels "in heaven", not of fallen ones who left their proper place (Jude 1:6).

The "sons of God" are the godly line of Seth (Gen 4:26; Gen 5) who intermarried with the ungodly line of Cain; the sin is religious compromise. It appears in Christian writing with Julius Africanus (early third century), was taken up by Ephrem, John Chrysostom and others, and became dominant in the West after Augustine (*City of God* 15.23), who thought angels could not father children; Luther and Calvin held it. Strengths: the passage is about human wickedness and judgment falls on humans. Critics note that Genesis never calls Seth's line "sons of God" and that "daughters of man" naturally means women generally.

The sons of God are kings or nobles (ancient kings were called sons of a god) who took women by force, perhaps building harems, and became tyrants ("men of renown"). Jewish tradition from the second century AD onward favoured readings like this: Targum Onkelos renders "sons of the great ones", and Genesis Rabbah 26.5 reports Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai cursing anyone who called them "sons of God" (meaning angels). Defended in modern times by Meredith Kline and others. Critics ask why the offspring would be singled out as Nephilim.

rebellions.title: Babel and the allotment of the nations
rebellions.who: The people of Shinar (Babylonia), building a city and a tower "with its top in the heavens", probably a ziggurat, a stepped temple-tower meant to link earth and heaven. On the council reading, also the heavenly beings to whom the scattered nations were then allotted.
rebellions.what: Humanity, told to fill the earth (Gen 9:1), instead gathers to "make a name for ourselves". Yahweh comes down, confuses their language and scatters them, and the city is called Babel (a pun on balal, "confuse"). Genesis 10 lists the resulting seventy nations. In Deut 32:8-9 (in its older form) the Most High divides the nations according to the number of the sons of God, but keeps Jacob as his portion; Deut 4:19-20 says the sun, moon and stars were "allotted to all the peoples" whereas Yahweh took Israel for himself.
rebellions.consequence: On the council reading, the nations are disinherited: given over to lesser gods who then demand worship and rule unjustly (Deut 32:17; Ps 82:2-5), which is why Israel is forbidden to worship the "host of heaven" and why Daniel sees angelic "princes" of Persia and Greece. On other readings, the consequence is simply the scattering of humankind into rival nations and languages, each falling into idolatry.
rebellions.reversal: God immediately calls Abraham, through whom "all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (Gen 12:3). At Pentecost the Spirit enables the apostles to speak in the languages of the nations, and Peter's hearers come from a long list of peoples (Acts 2:1-11); Paul tells the Athenians that God fixed the nations' boundaries so that they might seek him (Acts 17:26-27). Revelation ends with a great multitude "from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages" before the throne (Rev 7:9).

readings.text: Babel is a third rebellion: God judges it by giving the nations over to the sons of God, like handing people over to what they want (compare Rom 1:24). The gods of the nations are real but subordinate beings, and the rest of the Bible is about Yahweh taking the nations back. Held by Heiser and, in various forms, by many who accept the Qumran reading; it draws on wider studies of ancient "national gods" such as Daniel Block's *The Gods of the Nations* (1988).

Augustine (*City of God* 16.4-11) read Babel as the pride of the earthly city, which God humbled, while the City of God continued through Shem and Eber to Abraham. The classical view also generally held that angels watch over nations (a view traceable to Dan 10 and found in Origen and Pseudo-Dionysius) but without the idea that the nations' gods were the appointed angels gone bad.

Babel is a story explaining the variety of languages and mocking Babylon's ziggurats; Deut 32:8-9 preserves an older Israelite picture in which El Elyon (the Most High) gave each nation to one of his sons, Yahweh receiving Israel, before Yahweh and El were fully identified (Mark Smith and others). Many scholars dispute that the verse ever distinguished Yahweh from Elyon.

reclaim.text: Humanity's united rebellion ends with languages confused and peoples scattered into the seventy nations of Genesis 10. On the divine-council reading, the nations are also placed under the oversight of the sons of God; on other readings they simply drift into idolatry.

Immediately after Babel, God calls one man out of Mesopotamia and promises that "in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed". Paul calls this promise "the gospel preached beforehand to Abraham". The plan for the nations begins with one family.

Israel is Yahweh's "portion" and "allotted heritage", a "kingdom of priests" set among the nations. A priest stands between God and others, so Israel's calling was always meant to serve the wider world, not only itself.

The prophets speak to and about the nations: Jeremiah is a "prophet to the nations", Amos announces judgment on Israel's neighbours, Jonah preaches in Nineveh, and Isaiah foresees the nations streaming to Zion and even Egypt and Assyria called God's people alongside Israel.

"Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations." Isaiah expects God to punish "the host of heaven in heaven, and the kings of the earth on the earth", and Daniel sees dominion over all nations given to one like a son of man. Council readers call Ps 82:8 the thesis of the whole biblical story; others see it as one strong strand among several.

Jesus says the "ruler of this world" is being cast out; Paul says that at the cross God "disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame", and that the risen Christ sits "far above all rule and authority". Then the risen Jesus, now holding "all authority in heaven and on earth", sends his disciples to "all nations".

At Pentecost the Spirit gives speech in many languages, and Jews from across the known world hear God's works "in our own tongues". That Pentecost undoes Babel is an ancient and widely shared Christian reading. That Luke's list of peoples (Acts 2:9-11) was deliberately modelled on the Table of Nations in Gen 10 (argued by James M. Scott and others) is a hypothesis; many scholars think the list reflects the Jewish diaspora of Luke's day or an astrological geography instead.

Paul preaches "from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum" and plans to go on to Spain. Isaiah had foreseen messengers sent to the far nations, including Tarshish (probably in Spain), to declare God's glory. Some scholars (James M. Scott, Roger Aus, and popularly Heiser) suggest Paul was consciously working through the Table of Nations or Isaiah 66 toward the western edge of the world. This is an attractive hypothesis but Paul never says so; he gives practical reasons too (Rom 15:20-24). Whether he reached Spain is unknown; 1 Clement 5.7 says he went to "the limit of the west".

reclaim.stage: The powers subjected and the church as witness
reclaim.text: Through the church "the manifold wisdom of God" is made known "to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places"; Christ must reign until every rule, authority and power is subjected and every knee bows. On the council reading, a multinational church is a visible sign to the powers that their claim on the nations is over.

reclaim.stage: The nations healed and the sons of God restored
reclaim.text: In the new creation the kings of the earth bring the glory of the nations into the city, and the leaves of the tree of life are "for the healing of the nations". Believers, now "sons of God" by adoption (Rom 8:14-19; Gal 3:26), will judge angels and share Christ's throne. On the council reading, redeemed humans take the place in God's family once given to the failed sons of God; other interpreters describe the same texts as the restoration of humanity's original vocation to rule creation.

nations.name: Parthians
nations.gen10: No clear Genesis 10 counterpart; their homeland in north-east Iran lay beyond the peoples the Table names.
nations.note: Rome's great eastern rival in the first century; large Jewish communities lived in their empire, descended from the exiles. First in Luke's list, which runs roughly east to west.

nations.name: Medes
nations.gen10: Madai, a son of Japheth (Gen 10:2).
nations.note: Centred on Ecbatana (Hamadan). Israelite exiles were settled "in the cities of the Medes" (2 Kgs 17:6).

nations.name: Elamites
nations.gen10: Elam, first son of Shem (Gen 10:22).
nations.note: An ancient kingdom in south-west Iran around Susa. Elam had long ceased to exist as a state by Luke's day, which is one reason some scholars think Luke's list is modelled on older or biblical geography.

nations.name: Residents of Mesopotamia
nations.gen10: Asshur and Arphaxad, sons of Shem (Gen 10:22); Nimrod's cities in Shinar, including Babel (Gen 10:10-11).
nations.note: The land of Babel itself, and of Abraham's origins at Ur; home of the large Babylonian Jewish community.

nations.name: Judea
nations.gen10: The land of the Canaanite clans (Gen 10:15-19), later given to Abraham's descendants through Shem's line via Eber.
nations.note: Jerusalem is the starting point of the mission (Acts 1:8; Rom 15:19). Its inclusion in a list of foreign lands is a puzzle; some suggest it means greater Judea or is a scribal change.

nations.name: Cappadocia
nations.gen10: Josephus (*Antiquities* 1.6) linked the Cappadocians with Meshech, a son of Japheth (Gen 10:2); the identification is uncertain.
nations.note: Central Anatolia around Caesarea Mazaca (Kayseri). Addressed in 1 Pet 1:1.

nations.name: Pontus
nations.gen10: No secure Genesis 10 link; Josephus associated neighbouring Black Sea peoples with Riphath and Tiras (Gen 10:2-3).
nations.note: On the southern Black Sea coast; home of Aquila (Acts 18:2) and addressed in 1 Pet 1:1.

nations.name: Asia (Roman province)
nations.gen10: Lud, a son of Shem (Gen 10:22), traditionally identified with the Lydians of western Anatolia.
nations.note: Western Anatolia, capital Ephesus, where Paul spent over two years so that "all the residents of Asia heard the word" (Acts 19:10). Home of the seven churches of Rev 2–3.

nations.name: Phrygia
nations.gen10: Josephus linked Togarmah (Gen 10:3) with the Phrygians; uncertain.
nations.note: Inland Anatolia; Paul passed through "the region of Phrygia and Galatia" on his second and third journeys (Acts 16:6; Acts 18:23). Colossae and Laodicea lay in Phrygia.

nations.name: Pamphylia
nations.gen10: No clear Genesis 10 counterpart.
nations.note: The southern Anatolian coastal plain; Paul and Barnabas landed at Perga, where John Mark left them (Acts 13:13; Acts 14:24-25).

nations.name: Egypt
nations.gen10: Mizraim, a son of Ham (Gen 10:6, 10:13-14).
nations.note: Alexandria had one of the largest Jewish communities in the world and produced the Septuagint. Apollos came from there (Acts 18:24). Isaiah foresaw an altar to Yahweh in Egypt (Isa 19:19-25).

nations.name: Libya around Cyrene
nations.gen10: Put, a son of Ham (Gen 10:6), identified with Libya by Josephus and the Septuagint; also the Lehabim (Gen 10:13).
nations.note: Cyrene in modern eastern Libya had a large Jewish community; Simon who carried Jesus' cross came from there (Mark 15:21), and men of Cyrene first preached to Greeks at Antioch (Acts 11:20).

nations.name: Rome
nations.gen10: No direct Genesis 10 entry; later Jewish interpretation sometimes applied Kittim (Gen 10:4) to Rome (compare Dan 11:30, which the Greek renders "Romans").
nations.note: "Visitors from Rome" heard Peter at Pentecost; a church existed there before Paul arrived as a prisoner (Acts 28:14-16; Rom 1:7). Acts ends with Paul preaching there unhindered.

nations.name: Cretans
nations.gen10: Caphtorim (Gen 10:14), usually identified with Crete (compare Amos 9:7; Jer 47:4).
nations.note: Paul's ship sheltered at Fair Havens on Crete (Acts 27:7-13); Titus was left there to organise churches (Titus 1:5), implying a later visit.

nations.name: Arabians
nations.gen10: The sons of Joktan, such as Sheba and Havilah (Gen 10:26-30), and Cush's sons Seba and Dedan (Gen 10:7).
nations.note: Probably the Nabataean kingdom (capital Petra), south and east of Judea. Paul went "away into Arabia" after his conversion (Gal 1:17); what he did there is not stated.

nations.name: Tarshish / Spain
nations.gen10: Tarshish, son of Javan (Gen 10:4).
nations.note: Most scholars identify Tarshish with Tartessos in south-west Spain (near Huelva), though Sardinia and Tarsus have also been proposed. It was the farthest west Jonah could flee (Jonah 1:3) and is named in Isa 66:19 among the far nations. Paul planned to go to Spain (Rom 15:24, 28); whether he did is uncertain (1 Clement 5.7 says he reached "the limit of the west").

nations.name: Illyricum
nations.gen10: No clear Genesis 10 counterpart; it lay in the regions later Jewish geography gave to Japheth.
nations.note: The Roman province along the eastern Adriatic (roughly modern Albania to Croatia). Paul says he preached "as far as Illyricum" (Rom 15:19); whether he entered it or reached its border from Macedonia is debated. 2 Tim 4:10 mentions Titus going to Dalmatia, part of it.

nations.name: Macedonia
nations.gen10: Kittim (Gen 10:4) in one line of interpretation: 1 Maccabees 1:1 says Alexander came from "the land of Kittim".
nations.note: Entered after the vision of the man of Macedonia (Acts 16:9-10); churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. The first recorded church in Europe.

nations.name: Achaia
nations.gen10: Javan (Gen 10:2), the Ionian Greeks; Elishah (Gen 10:4) is also sometimes placed in Greece.
nations.note: Southern Greece, capital Corinth, where Paul stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11); also Athens (Acts 17:16-34).

nations.name: Galatia
nations.gen10: Gomer, son of Japheth (Gen 10:2), whom Josephus identified with the Galatians (Gauls).
nations.note: Central Anatolia (capital Ancyra/Ankara); the Roman province also included Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Paul wrote Galatians to churches there; whether north or south Galatia is meant is debated.

nations.name: Cyprus
nations.gen10: Kittim, son of Javan (Gen 10:4), named after Kition on Cyprus; Elishah may also be Cyprus (Alashiya).
nations.note: Barnabas's home (Acts 4:36) and the first stop of the first journey, from Salamis to Paphos, where the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed (Acts 13:4-12).

nations.name: Cilicia / Tarsus
nations.gen10: Josephus linked Tarshish (Gen 10:4) with Tarsus; most modern scholars prefer a western site for Tarshish.
nations.note: Paul's home city (Acts 21:39; Acts 22:3); he worked in "Syria and Cilicia" for years before the recorded journeys (Gal 1:21).

nations.name: Cush / Ethiopia
nations.gen10: Cush, son of Ham (Gen 10:6-8).
nations.note: The Nubian kingdom of Meroë on the upper Nile, south of Egypt. The gospel reached it through the Ethiopian official baptised by Philip (Acts 8:26-39), whom some read as fulfilling Ps 68:31.

objections.question: Isn't a divine council just polytheism?
objections.answer: Council readers say no. Polytheism means worshipping many gods who share power and often have their own origins. In the Bible the council members are created (Neh 9:6; Ps 148:2-5; Col 1:16), owe Yahweh worship (Ps 29:1-2; Ps 97:7), can be judged and sentenced to die (Ps 82:7), and Israel may worship none of them (Exod 20:3). Yahweh is unique in kind: the only uncreated one, the Creator of the rest. Heiser summed it up as "Yahweh is an elohim, but no other elohim is Yahweh"; scholars often use terms like "monolatry" (worship of one God) or speak of Yahweh's "incomparability".
objections.otherViews: Classical theists agree the Bible forbids worship of other beings but prefer to call the council members "angels" and avoid the word "gods" except for idols or as figurative language, worried that loose talk of "gods" blurs the Creator–creature line. Historical critics such as Mark Smith argue that some older texts (e.g. Deut 32:8-9 in its older form, Ps 82) do reflect a real early Israelite polytheism or henotheism, which later writers reinterpreted. Nathan MacDonald argues that "monotheism" (a 17th-century term) is a poor label for Deuteronomy, whose concern is exclusive loyalty to Yahweh, not abstract counting of gods.

objections.question: Doesn't the Shema say there is only one God?
objections.answer: The Shema (Deut 6:4) can be translated "Yahweh our God, Yahweh is one" or "Yahweh is our God, Yahweh alone." Many scholars think its main point is exclusive loyalty: Israel must love Yahweh alone with all its heart (Deut 6:5). The same book says Yahweh is "God of gods" (Deut 10:17) and warns against serving other gods (Deut 6:14), and also says "there is no other besides him" (Deut 4:35, 39). Council readers take these together as saying Yahweh is unique and supreme, not that no other spiritual beings exist.
objections.otherViews: Jewish and Christian tradition has long read the Shema as a confession of the oneness of God, and many scholars read Deut 4:35, 39 as a clear denial that other gods are real gods at all. Christians also note that Paul rewrites the Shema to include Jesus (1 Cor 8:6), which Bauckham calls "christological monotheism". Critical scholars often think Deut 4 is a later (exilic) layer that moves toward stricter monotheism than the earlier chapters.

objections.question: What about "there is no god besides me" in Isaiah?
objections.answer: Isaiah 40–48 repeatedly says "there is no other" and "besides me there is no god" (Isa 45:5; 46:9). Council readers note that Babylon says almost the same words of herself, "I am, and there is no one besides me" (Isa 47:8, 10), and so does Nineveh (Zeph 2:15). Babylon did not mean no other cities existed; she meant none could compare. So, they argue, the phrase is a claim of incomparability: no other being is like Yahweh in power, knowledge of the future or ability to save.
objections.otherViews: Many scholars read Second Isaiah as the Bible's first explicit, theoretical monotheism: the idols are "nothing" (Isa 41:24, 29), made from half a log used for firewood (Isa 44:9-20), and "before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me" (Isa 43:10). On this view the comparison with Isa 47:8 shows the same boast, but the context makes Yahweh's claim stronger. Some suggest a middle way: Isaiah denies that any other being is truly "god" in the sense of creator and saviour, while not denying heavenly beings exist.

objections.question: Aren't the "gods" of Psalm 82 just human judges?
objections.answer: Most modern commentators think not. The psalm sets the scene in "the council of El", contrasts the gods with humans ("you will die like men" and "fall like any prince"), and ends by asking God to judge "the earth" and inherit "all the nations", which fits beings with authority over nations, not Israelite magistrates. Hans-Joachim Kraus's Psalms commentary, for example, rejects the human-judges view. Divine beings held responsible for justice on earth also fits Isa 24:21 and Dan 10.
objections.otherViews: The human-judges view has a long history among Jewish and Christian interpreters (including Calvin and many Puritans) and is still held by some evangelical scholars. Its supporters point to texts where elohim may mean judges (Exod 21:6; Exod 22:8-9), to the purely human sins named (partiality, neglect of orphans), and to Jesus' comment that those "to whom the word of God came" were called gods (John 10:35), which seems to describe humans. Others read the psalm as addressed to Israel at Sinai, or to foreign kings who claimed divinity.

objections.question: How does Jesus' quotation in John 10:34-36 work?
objections.answer: Accused of blasphemy for claiming to be God's Son, Jesus quotes Ps 82:6, "I said, you are gods", and argues from lesser to greater: if Scripture called others "gods", how can it be blasphemy for the one the Father consecrated and sent to say "I am the Son of God"? Council readers think Jesus refers to the divine beings of Ps 82, and that his point is that Scripture already knows of plural elohim and of a Son with a unique role; the phrase "to whom the word of God came" refers to the beings God addressed in the psalm.
objections.otherViews: Many commentators think Jesus means human judges or leaders who received God's word, so his argument is: even humans can be called "gods" in Scripture, so the title alone is no blasphemy. Others (e.g. Jerome Neyrey) argue for the rabbinic reading that the psalm addresses Israel at Sinai, who received God's word (the law). All agree the argument is not that Jesus is merely one god among many; John's Gospel presents him as uniquely one with the Father (John 10:30; John 1:1).

objections.question: Are demons the spirits of the dead Nephilim?
objections.answer: This idea is stated in 1 Enoch 15:8-12: when the giants died, evil spirits came out of their bodies and roam the earth. It was widely believed in Second Temple Judaism and by some early Christian writers (e.g. Justin Martyr, Athenagoras). Heiser and others suggest it may explain why demons in the Gospels seek bodies to inhabit (Matt 12:43-45) and why they are distinguished from fallen angels kept in chains (Jude 1:6). It should be labelled clearly: the Bible itself never says where demons come from.
objections.otherViews: The dominant Christian view (Augustine, Aquinas, the Reformers, most theologians today) is that demons are fallen angels who followed Satan (based on Matt 25:41; Rev 12:7-9). Others treat the Bible's language about demons as reflecting the world-view of its time without settling their origin, and some scholars see the Enochic story as a way Jewish writers explained the origin of evil without blaming humans alone. The Old Testament's "demons" (shedim, Deut 32:17; Ps 106:37) are identified with the gods of the nations, not with Nephilim.

objections.question: Did Israel's religion evolve from polytheism?
objections.answer: Council readers argue that the Bible's council is not a leftover from polytheism but a deliberate part of its theology, carried into the New Testament (Eph 6:12; Col 1:16). They accept that many Israelites worshipped other gods (the Bible says so constantly), but distinguish what the people did from what the biblical writers taught. They also note that Yahweh is presented as unique even in old poetry such as Exod 15:11 ("Who is like you among the gods?").
objections.otherViews: Many historians (Mark Smith, Rainer Albertz and others) argue that early Israelite religion included El, Yahweh, Baal and Asherah; that Yahweh absorbed El's roles and titles; and that strict monotheism emerged late, around the exile. Evidence includes inscriptions such as "Yahweh and his asherah" at Kuntillet Ajrud, the prophets' own complaints (Jer 11:13), and Josiah's reforms (2 Kgs 23:4-14). Yehezkel Kaufmann, by contrast, argued Israel's religion was monotheistic from the start and that popular idolatry was a corruption. Many scholars today take a middle position: official Yahweh-only worship coexisted with widespread folk religion, and the writers' convictions sharpened over time.

objections.question: If idols are "nothing", how can the gods be real?
objections.answer: Paul holds both together: "an idol has no real existence" and "there is no God but one" (1 Cor 8:4), yet "what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God" (1 Cor 10:20). He is echoing Deut 32:17, which calls the nations' gods shedim (demons) and "not God". Council readers see a consistent picture: the statue is just wood or stone, but real spiritual powers can stand behind the cult; they are "by nature not gods" (Gal 4:8) in the full sense, because only the Creator is God.
objections.otherViews: Some interpreters read Paul's "demons" as a way of saying idolatry is spiritually destructive rather than as a claim about beings behind each idol, and read the Old Testament's mockery of idols (Isa 44; Jer 10:3-5) as denying any reality to the gods at all. Classical theology generally accepted that demons can exploit idol worship while insisting the "gods" as such are false.

scholars.name: H. Wheeler Robinson
scholars.work: "The Council of Yahweh", *Journal of Theological Studies* 45
scholars.contribution: An early, influential article arguing that the Old Testament pictures Yahweh surrounded by a heavenly court, and that the prophets claimed to have stood in it (Jer 23:18, 22). It put the council on the agenda of modern Old Testament study.

scholars.name: Frank Moore Cross
scholars.contribution: Compared Ugaritic myths about El, his assembly and Baal with Israel's poetry and prophecy, arguing that Yahweh took over many of El's features and that the prophet was a messenger of the divine council. Shaped a generation of Harvard-trained scholars.

scholars.name: Patrick D. Miller
scholars.work: "Cosmology and World Order in the Old Testament: The Divine Council as Cosmic-Political Symbol"; earlier *The Divine Warrior in Early Israel* (1973)
scholars.contribution: Showed how the council works in the Old Testament as a picture of God's government of the world, linking heavenly decisions to justice on earth (as in Ps 82), and traced the heavenly host as Yahweh's army.

scholars.name: E. Theodore Mullen Jr.
scholars.work: *The Assembly of the Gods: The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature*
scholars.contribution: The first full-length study comparing the council of El at Ugarit with the council of Yahweh in the Hebrew Bible, covering its members, meeting places and functions.

scholars.name: Mark S. Smith
scholars.work: *The Origins of Biblical Monotheism*; also *The Early History of God* (1990, 2nd ed. 2002)
scholars.contribution: Argues that Israel's religion developed from a family-style pantheon (El, his sons, Yahweh, Baal, Asherah) to monolatry and finally to explicit monotheism around the exile, with the council texts as traces of the earlier stages. The leading evolutionary account, widely respected but disputed by more traditional scholars.

scholars.name: Michael S. Heiser
scholars.work: *The Unseen Realm*; doctoral dissertation (University of Wisconsin–Madison, 2004) on the divine council in late canonical and Second Temple Jewish literature
scholars.contribution: Synthesised the council material into a whole-Bible theology for a popular evangelical audience: the three rebellions, the Deut 32 "cosmic geography" of nations under lesser gods, and the New Testament as the reclaiming of the nations. Very influential at the popular level; critics say it builds a large system on a few texts and sometimes treats possible readings as settled.

scholars.name: Ronald S. Hendel
scholars.work: "Of Demigods and the Deluge: Toward an Interpretation of Genesis 6:1-4", *Journal of Biblical Literature* 106
scholars.contribution: Argued that Gen 6:1-4 is a short myth of divine beings mating with women, related to ancient Near Eastern and Greek stories of demigods, and that the flood answers the blurring of the boundary between gods and humans.

scholars.name: Larry W. Hurtado
scholars.work: *One God, One Lord: Early Christian Devotion and Ancient Jewish Monotheism*; later *Lord Jesus Christ* (2003)
scholars.contribution: Showed that Second Temple Judaism, while speaking of many angelic beings and exalted figures, reserved worship for God alone, and that the earliest Christians strikingly included Jesus in that worship. Key for seeing where Jesus fits relative to the council.

scholars.name: Richard Bauckham
scholars.work: *Jesus and the God of Israel* (expanding *God Crucified*, 1998)
scholars.contribution: Argues that Jewish monotheism was defined by God's unique identity (sole Creator and sole Ruler over all, to whom alone worship is due) and that the New Testament places Jesus within that identity, not among the angels or council members. A strong counterweight to readings that make Christ one exalted being among many.

scholars.name: Ellen White
scholars.contribution: Questions models that divide the council into fixed tiers borrowed from Ugarit (such as Lowell Handy's four-level pantheon), arguing that the biblical texts show a looser and more varied picture. Her work is a useful check on neat "three-tier" schemes, including popular ones.
